source.title_on_document: Cueing the Crowd: LLM-Driven Conversational Cues Across Different Meeting Modalities Increase Topical Diversity of Generated Ideas

supplement.where: Appendix A.1 'Supplemental Materials' (PDF p. 15, printed p. 310): https://osf.io/nmqd5/files/osfstorage?view_only=0b6efc5a1bf3466395292501cd52de2f. The rest of Appendix A (task instructions, prompts, homogenization analysis, survey questions) is in this PDF, printed pp. 310-316.
supplement.holds: Data. A.1 says 'The data for this project can be found in this link' and names no extra statistics. Arm counts (dyads or people per condition), standard errors, and the result of the idea-homogenization test appear nowhere in the PDF; they would have to come from the OSF data.

paper_design_summary: 172 participants (a majority took part for course credit; almost all were psychology or cognitive science students) were randomly assigned to a 2 x 2 between-subjects lab experiment and brainstormed in 86 dyads for 20 minutes on alternative uses for recyclable trash from a beach cleanup. Dyads in the Cue arms received a short GPT-4o-mini cue about once a minute (the CueTip system), generated from the live transcript; NoCue dyads received none; dyads met either in person or over video. The authors scored each dyad's ideas for topic diversity (BERTopic topics, Shannon entropy) and number, scored each dyad's conversation transcript for the number of distinct IAB topics, and compared each idea's cosine distance to an average idea embedding, which the paper describes both per condition and pooled over both arms (figure only); a model-only analysis compared the original cues with cues regenerated by a Wikipedia-based pipeline.

studies.label: 2 x 2 lab experiment: LLM conversational cues (Cue vs NoCue) x meeting modality (in-person vs virtual), dyadic brainstorming

assignment.what_was_assigned: One of four conditions: Cue-Virtual, Cue-InPerson, NoCue-Virtual, NoCue-InPerson. Cue arms received a GPT-4o-mini cue about once a minute during the 20-minute ideation task; NoCue arms received none. The paper says participants were randomly assigned. Both members of a dyad share one condition. The REML analyses use one score per dyad, and the homogenization test compares idea-level distances. The pre-survey collected demographics and background 'for balancing across conditions', and conditions were balanced for gender and age; the allocation procedure itself is not described.
assignment.quote: We recruited 172 participants, randomly assigned to four conditions; Cue-Virtual, Cue-InPerson, NoCue-Virtual, and NoCue-InPerson to participate in a brainstorming discussion with one other participant (in 86 dyads).
assignment.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 300), Sec. 4.1.1; also Sec. 4 opening (PDF p. 5), Sec. 1 (PDF p. 3, dyads assigned to conditions), and Sec. 8 (PDF p. 11)

participants.exclusions: Four sessions were dropped: two discussions were 'removed and excluded from the analysis' because of echoes in the audio recordings, and two other sessions were dropped for technical issues (PDF p. 5). Thirteen participants who did not report prior design experience and prior topic knowledge were excluded from analyses that account for these factors; the REML models include both as random effects (PDF pp. 5 and 7). Footnote 12: the audio comes from 70 sessions; 4 were excluded from the conversation analysis for echoes, and 16 recordings were not included because the screen recorder captured only the researcher (PDF p. 7). The footnote does not say whether the 16 recordings are among the 70 sessions (70 + 16 = 86, the number of dyads). Two sessions were excluded from the cue-noticing coding (PDF p. 7). The paper never states the number of people or dyads analyzed in any analysis or in any arm. The REML F tests have denominator df 67.03 (ideas) and 50.76 (conversation). With four fixed-effect parameters, these imply at least about 71 and 55 dyads analyzed (an inference, not a printed count).
participants.who: Ages 18 to 37 (median 21); 42 male, 127 female, 3 non-binary; compensated with course credit or $20 for 75 minutes. The limitations section says a majority took part for research credit and almost all were in psychology or cognitive science.
participants.country: not stated (lab study; all authors at the University of California, San Diego)
participants.quote: A majority of the participants in our study participated for research credit. This may have contributed to a selection bias because almost all of the participants were in psychology or cognitive science.
participants.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 300), Sec. 4.1.1; PDF p. 11 (printed p. 306), Sec. 7; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 302), footnote 12

ai_tool.name_model: CueTip system using OpenAI GPT-4o-mini; live transcription from the Daily.js call frame
ai_tool.how_used: Every minute, CueTip prompted GPT-4o-mini with a summary of the conversation, the last ten utterances, and the previous cues, and asked for one divergence cue (Sec. 3.2.2: 'less than five words'; the prompt: 'not be longer than five words'), e.g., 'What if we created furniture?'. Each cue appeared in a cue panel with a visual notification and an audio chime, above a cue history; about 18 +/- 2 cues per session. Cues arrived on a fixed schedule, and participants could not request them (Sec. 5.3.3). Fig. 1 also shows 'Notes from Ideators' as an input to cue generation. App. A.3.1 gives a separate prompt for familiarity-building cues, and A.3 introduces it among 'the prompts that we used'. Every dyad did a familiarity-building task before the ideation task, but the main text counts cues only for the 20-minute ideation conversation and does not say whether Cue dyads also received cues during the familiarity-building task.

task.description: Dyadic verbal brainstorming, described as an alternative uses task: come up with as many alternative uses as possible to repurpose recyclable trash uncovered during a beach cleanup, listing ideas as bullet points in shared notes; the first 15 minutes for generating ideas, the last 5 for selecting the best one. A familiarity-building task came first.
task.duration: 20-minute ideation task (15 minutes generating, 5 selecting) in a 75-minute session

outcomes.name: Topic diversity of generated ideas (BERTopic topics, Shannon entropy; one score per dyad)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Ideas from all groups pooled and fit with BERTopic, HDBSCAN clustering (minimum cluster size 15); Shannon entropy (scipy) gives the topic diversity score. The text says entropy gives 'each idea's topic diversity score', but Fig. 5a and the REML model (denominator df 67.03) use one score per dyad. Coded flexibility because it measures topical variety within one dyad's ideas, not similarity across dyads; coded category_count because topics come from clustering (the score is an entropy, not a count). Model: REML with Access-to-Cue, Modality, and their interaction as fixed effects; prior design experience and recycling knowledge (group-level 0/1/2) as random effects; Tukey HSD post hoc. Sec. 5.1.1 says 'The topic diversity of cues served as the dependent variable', apparently a slip for ideas.

contrasts.reported: Cues μ = 2.3, SD = 0.3 vs without cues μ = 2.1, SD = 0.4 (arm ns not printed); REML Access-to-Cue F(1, 67.03) = 6.51, p = 0.013; Tukey HSD p ≈ 0.012 (Fig. 5a caption: p = 0.012). Modality F(1, 67.17) = 0.79, p = 0.38; no cue x modality interaction found (no statistic printed). Fig. 5a box plot: Cue Max 2.784, Q3 2.525, Med 2.351, Q1 2.095, Min 1.494; Without Cue Max 2.805, Q3 2.322, Med 2.098, Q1 1.839, Min 1.075.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 302), Sec. 5.1.1; PDF p. 8 (printed p. 303), Fig. 5a

outcomes.name: Topic diversity of the conversation transcript (number of unique IAB Level-1 topics per dyad)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Ideation conversation audio transcribed with AssemblyAI; utterances mapped to the 698 Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB) topics; for each speaker and round, the number of unique Level-1 topics; the combined set of unique Level-1 topics across rounds is the dyad's score. Scored on all words spoken in the discussion, not on the listed ideas, so the construct is coded 'other' (topic variety of the dyad's spoken discussion) rather than flexibility. Same REML model and Tukey HSD as S1-O1. Footnote 12: audio from 70 sessions, 4 excluded for echoes, 16 not included because only the researcher was recorded. The footnote does not say whether the 16 are among the 70. If they are, at most 50 sessions enter this analysis; if not, at most 66. The denominator df of 50.76 (at least about 55 dyads with four fixed-effect parameters) fit the second reading.

contrasts.reported: Cues μ = 9.6, SD = 2.2 vs without cues μ = 8.0, SD = 2.5 (arm ns not printed); REML Access-to-Cue F(1, 50.76) = 6.25, p = 0.016; Tukey HSD p ≈ 0.015 (Fig. 5b caption: p ≈ 0.015). Modality F(1, 50.79) = 0.25, p = 0.62; no cue x modality interaction found. Fig. 5b box plot (number of unique topics): Cue Max 14.00, Q3 11.00, Med 9.00, Q1 7.50, Min 6.00; Without Cue Max 14.00, Q3 9.00, Med 8.00, Q1 6.00, Min 3.00.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 9 (printed p. 304), Sec. 5.1.2; PDF p. 8 (printed p. 303), Fig. 5b; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 302), Sec. 4.1.4 and footnote 12

outcomes.name: Number of ideas per dyad
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: A research team member removed duplicates from each session's raw notes (unclear cases discussed with a second member); team members filled in missing ideas from the recording and transcript; the score is the number of points in each classified note. Same REML model as S1-O1. Dyads averaged 19.4 ideas across all groups.

contrasts.reported: 'None of the factors showed a significant difference based on the REML model.' No arm means, test statistics, or p-values printed. Overall average 19.4 ideas per dyad (Sec. 5).
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 9 (printed p. 304), Sec. 5.1.3; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 302), Sec. 5

outcomes.name: Homogenization of ideas across groups: cosine distance of each idea to an average idea embedding (per condition in Sec. 6.3, pooled over both arms in App. A.4.1)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Following Anderson, Shah and Kreminski (2024) [4]: the cosine distance (scikit-learn pairwise distances, footnote 16) between each idea embedding and an average idea embedding, with Cue and NoCue ideas compared by a Wilcoxon test 'on the Access-to-Cue factor'. The paper describes the average two ways. Sec. 6.3 uses 'the average embedding of all ideas within each condition'. App. A.4.1 builds 'the average embedding based on ideas across groups' and takes distances to 'idea embeddings from both Cue and NoCue groups', which reads as one centroid pooled over both arms, and App. A.4.2 says the cue analysis was set up like the idea analysis and aggregated both cue sets into one average. The paper does not settle which centroid was used or how modality enters it. Fig. 6 shows two violins, Cue Ideas and No Cue Ideas, so the comparison pools the two modalities. Higher distance means more spread. With a pooled centroid, the distance mixes spread within an arm with the gap between the arm means. The text calls the quantity 'cosine similarity', but Fig. 6 plots distance.

contrasts.reported: No test statistic, p-value, mean, or n is printed for ideas. Sec. 6.3 names the Wilcoxon test and then reports only that 'across groups, participants were exposed to semantically similar cues' (182 of 578 divergence cues repeated verbatim in other groups). Fig. 6 ('Distribution of Cosine Distances: Cue vs No-Cue Ideas') is the only evidence: the violins overlap, with medians about 0.55 (Cue) and 0.56 (No Cue) and quartile bars about 0.47-0.64 (Cue) and 0.46-0.67 (No Cue), all read from the figure, not printed. The caption does not say which arm is more concentrated. Direction coded from the figure; the paper states none.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 11 (printed p. 306), Sec. 6.3; PDF p. 16 (printed p. 311), App. A.4.1; PDF p. 17 (printed p. 312), Fig. 6

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine distance between each idea embedding and an average idea embedding: the average of all ideas within each condition (Sec. 6.3) or one average over ideas from both arms (App. A.4.1); the paper does not settle which
diversity_detail.computed_over: each output against a centroid: its condition's centroid per Sec. 6.3, or one centroid of all Cue and NoCue ideas per App. A.4.1 (the paper does not settle which)
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Wilcoxon test on idea-level distances named; result not printed
diversity_detail.notes: The paper's homogenization narrative rests on cue repetition, not on a reported test of ideas: the introduction says 'we observe a homogenization effect [4] across groups where similar cues are generated for group after group' (PDF p. 3). Fig. 6 values were read from the embedded raster image against its axis ticks (0.3 to 1.0). The paper describes the centroid two ways (Sec. 6.3 per condition, App. A.4.1 pooled over both arms); open_questions lists the conflict.

outcomes.name: Homogeneity of cues: cosine distance of each cue to an average cue embedding (per version in Sec. 6.3, pooled over both versions in App. A.4.2)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Scored on AI-generated cues, not on participant output. Metric: cosine distance between each cue embedding and an average cue embedding. The paper describes the average two ways. Sec. 6.3 uses 'the average embedding of all cues within each condition' (one centroid per version, regular vs pipeline). App. A.4.2 says the authors 'calculated the average embedding of cues, by aggregating cues generated during the study, and by the new pipeline' and took distances 'to both groups' from it (one centroid pooled over both versions). The paper does not settle which. Embedding model not stated; Wilcoxon test over cue-level scores. The text calls the quantity 'cosine similarity', but Fig. 10 plots cosine distance, and the conclusion (regular cues 'more homogeneous' at 0.46 vs 0.54) fits distance. Construct coded 'other' because the codebook reserves diversity for different people's outputs, so diversity_detail stays empty.

contrasts.reported: 'the cues generated without the pipeline (μ=0.46, SD=0.11) were significantly (p < 0.0001) more homogeneous than those generated with the pipeline (μ=0.54, SD=0.23)'. Number of cues per version not printed (578 divergence cues were sent in the study, 182 repeated verbatim in other groups). Fig. 10 plots cosine distance by cue type (Regular vs Pipeline). Direction refers to spread: pipeline cues are more diverse.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 11 (printed p. 306), Sec. 6.3; PDF p. 19 (printed p. 314), Fig. 10

eligibility.reason: S1 randomly assigned 172 participants, who worked in 86 dyads that shared a condition, to receive GPT-4o-mini conversational cues about once a minute or no cues during a 20-minute alternative-uses brainstorm (PDF p. 5, printed p. 300, Secs. 4 and 4.1.1; PDF p. 11, Sec. 8). The ideas the dyads wrote were scored by computed measures: BERTopic topic entropy, idea counts, and idea-to-centroid cosine distance. The paper prints no count of people analyzed. Four sessions were dropped, and 13 participants lacked the covariates used in the REML models. By arithmetic on these exclusions (not a printed count), at least 69 dyads (138 people) were analyzed for the idea outcomes, so criterion 2 is met on any reading. The ideas REML denominator df (67.03) imply at least about 71 dyads. Criterion 2 does not rest on the conversation outcome. Footnote 12 leaves its sample unclear: at most 50 sessions if the 16 researcher-only recordings are among the 70 audio sessions and at most 66 if not, and the denominator df (50.76) fit the larger number. The condition is shared within each dyad and the REML analyses use one score per dyad, so the independent units are dyads. S2 is a model-only cue comparison.

one_line_finding: Dyads that received GPT-4o-mini cues produced ideas with higher topic diversity (entropy 2.3, SD 0.3 vs 2.1, SD 0.4; F(1, 67.03) = 6.51, p = 0.013) and conversations covering more topics (9.6 vs 8.0 unique topics; F(1, 50.76) = 6.25, p = 0.016), with no significant difference in the number of ideas and no printed test of across-group homogenization (PDF pp. 7-9, Sec. 5.1, Fig. 5; PDF p. 17, Fig. 6).
open_questions: The number of people and dyads analyzed, per arm and per outcome, is not stated anywhere. With four fixed-effect parameters, the REML denominator df (67.03 for ideas, 50.76 for conversation) imply at least about 71 and 55 dyads (an inference, not a printed count). Footnote 12 does not say whether the 16 researcher-only recordings are among the 70 audio sessions: at most 50 sessions enter the conversation analysis if they are, at most 66 if not, and the df fit the second reading. The arithmetic lower bound for the idea outcomes (69 dyads, 138 people) holds either way. The OSF data would settle it.
The Wilcoxon test of idea homogenization (Sec. 6.3, App. A.4.1) has no printed result; Fig. 6 is the only evidence, and the direction code rests on reading it.

Topic diversity of ideas: the text says entropy gives 'each idea's topic diversity score', but Fig. 5a and the REML df imply one score per dyad. Whether the dyad score is the entropy of the dyad's topic distribution or an average of per-idea entropies is not stated; this bears on the flexibility coding.
Whether within-dyad topic entropy is best coded as flexibility (as here) or as diversity; the paper calls it 'topic diversity'.
Whether the conversation transcript counts as the participants' output for criterion 3. Eligibility does not depend on it, because the idea outcomes qualify.
Role coded ideas_supplied: cues such as 'What if we created furniture?' name content directions; a reviewer could argue for coach or other.
Sec. 5.1.1 names 'the topic diversity of cues' as the dependent variable, apparently a slip for ideas.

Allocation: the paper says participants were 'randomly assigned', but the pre-survey also served 'balancing across conditions'; whether allocation was simple, blocked, or balanced by hand is not described.

Centroid of the homogenization measures (S1-O4, S2-O1): Sec. 6.3 compares each idea with 'the average embedding of all ideas within each condition' and each cue with 'the average embedding of all cues within each condition', but App. A.4.1 and A.4.2 describe one average embedding pooled over Cue and NoCue ideas and one pooled over both cue versions. Which centroid was used decides whether the distances measure spread within an arm or distance to the grand mean.

Familiarity-building cues: App. A.3.1 gives a prompt for familiarity-building cues, listed among 'the prompts that we used', but the main text counts cues only for the 20-minute ideation task. Whether Cue dyads also received cues during the familiarity-building task is not stated.
notes: Outcome ids follow the paper's order (as in B): final S1-O1 = A S1-O1 = B S1-O1 (topic diversity of ideas); final S1-O2 = A S1-O3 = B S1-O2 (conversation topic diversity); final S1-O3 = A S1-O4 = B S1-O3 (number of ideas); final S1-O4 = A S1-O2 = B S1-O4 (idea homogenization). Not listed as outcomes: the cue noticing rate (InPerson μ = 15.0, SD = 3.1 vs Virtual μ = 14.2, SD = 4.2; Wilcoxon p ≈ 0.88; PDF p. 9, Sec. 5.2), which compares modalities within the Cue arms; Spearman correlations between attended cues and idea topic diversity (p ≈ 0.024, rs ≈ 0.35) and number of ideas (p ≈ 0.074, rs ≈ 0.28; virtual Cue groups p ≈ 0.0024, rs ≈ 0.63) (PDF p. 9, Secs. 5.2.1-5.2.2), which are not randomized contrasts; post-survey Likert and think-aloud answers (self-report, reported qualitatively, Sec. 5.3). Modality (in-person vs virtual) is a second randomized factor but not an AI contrast; its main effects on idea and conversation topic diversity were not significant, and no cue x modality interaction was found. The authors did not use expert raters for novelty, creativity, or feasibility 'due to the large number of ideas' (PDF p. 7, Sec. 5.1). A pilot with N=10 users (5 dyads) informed the design (PDF p. 4, Sec. 3.1). Fig. 4 shows the ideation prompt as a 'valley cleanup', while the text and Appendix A.2.2 say beach cleanup. No preregistration is mentioned anywhere in the paper.
